section_summary: This section documents Allied efforts in mid-1941 to restrict Japan’s access to petroleum, mercury, manganese, molybdenum, platinum, industrial diamonds and other strategic materials. Its central document is a lengthy State Department review explaining why the United States had gradually tightened oil controls while postponing a complete embargo to gain time for rearmament and avoid provoking Japanese expansion into the Netherlands East Indies. The remaining correspondence and reports trace Japanese procurement and barter efforts across Latin America, together with British, American and local efforts to block or redirect those transactions.

subfiles.title: Garbled mercury-quantity calculation and annotation
subfiles.about: A handwritten annotation attempts to reconcile garbled quantities and values in a mercury telegram.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten note on a garbled mercury telegram: flask weight about 96 pounds and value about 180-200 pounds sterling each.

subfiles.title: Telegram on mercury aboard SS Mar Cantabrico
subfiles.about: Reports a large mercury shipment routed from Cádiz through Buenos Aires for Mitsui in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: SS Mar Cantabrico reportedly left Cádiz July 25 with 120 tons of mercury for Mitsui, Tokyo; sources give inconsistent quantities.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on diesel oil for Japanese vessels in Peru
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Peru’s revised bunkering rules adequately prevent Japanese ships from obtaining excess fuel.
subfiles.summary: Memo on a Santiago report of 1,500 tons of diesel oil for Japanese vessels in Peru: probably bunkers, and new Peruvian limits to the next port of call suffice, so no action.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Peruvian diesel-oil sale to Japanese ships
subfiles.about: Reports a Peruvian government sale of diesel oil to the Japanese ships Kunikawa and Norfolk Maru.
subfiles.summary: Peru reportedly arranged to sell 2,000 tons of diesel oil to the Kunikawa and Norfolk Maru, 1,500 apparently as cargo, delivered at Los Cerritos.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Naval Attaché report on Peruvian bunkering restrictions
subfiles.doc_type: paraphrased naval telegram with routing sheet
subfiles.to: U.S. naval and State Department officials
subfiles.about: Explains Peru’s inspection and approval requirements for supplying oil to Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: The Peruvian Government would provide no oil to Japanese vessels without approval from the Ministry of War and an inspection by the captain of the port. Approved vessels would receive only enough fuel to reach the next fueling port, and ships refusing inspection would receive none.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on manganese exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Describes the tightening of British restrictions on manganese exports from India and Malaya to Japan.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy: manganese quotas for Japan were 10,000 tons from India and 1,700 from Malaya, then halved; after freezing, licenses mostly denied; little Indian manganese moves; Malaya complicated by Japanese-owned mines.

subfiles.title: Finletter letter to Will Clayton on mica shipments
subfiles.about: Promises to raise the serious issue of Indian mica shipments to Japan with the British Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Finletter tells Clayton the Indian mica exports to Japan are serious and he will raise them with the British Embassy immediately.

subfiles.title: Oil Shipments to Japan: A Survey of This Government’s Policy
subfiles.about: Reviews the political, strategic, legal and economic reasoning behind the gradual restriction of American oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces American Far Eastern policy from Japan’s seizure of Manchuria through the war in China, the European war and Japan’s expansion toward French Indochina. It explains that public opposition to sanctions, treaty and commercial-law concerns, the need for cooperation from other oil producers and military warnings against simultaneous Atlantic and Pacific wars initially militated against a complete embargo. Washington instead imposed licensing controls, stopped aviation-gasoline exports, strengthened American, British and Dutch defenses and aided China while gaining time for rearmament. By mid-1941, Japan’s worsening strategic position and the German attack on the Soviet Union made stronger measures, including asset freezing and a possible oil embargo, less likely to trigger an immediate seizure of the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: Code radiogram on Japanese troop movements near Canton and Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese troop strength near Canton and Hong Kong and movements toward Cambodia.
subfiles.summary: Radiogram: most of Japan's 18th Division remains near Canton and Hong Kong; British sources say about one division and one brigade of the 104th moved to Cambodia.

subfiles.title: Senator Thomas letter requesting an answer for Parke S. Petterson
subfiles.about: Requests a State Department response to a constituent’s questions about American policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Thomas forwards Parke Petterson's letter and asks Green for a reply explaining Japan policy.

subfiles.title: Parke S. Petterson letter criticizing supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Challenges Senator Thomas to explain continued American exports of oil, scrap iron and munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Petterson accuses policymakers of appeasing Japan with strategic shipments, questions exports after Japan joined the Axis, and asks for a clear explanation.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Thomas on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Responds to Petterson’s criticism by outlining existing restrictions and the recent change in oil policy.
subfiles.summary: Reply denies militarily important goods flowed unrestricted: exports limited to prewar quantities and being curtailed, scrap virtually embargoed since October 16, 1940; cites the President's explanation and encloses the August 1 announcement.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with George S. Walden on petroleum exports
subfiles.about: Records guidance given to Standard-Vacuum concerning petroleum shipments from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiss informed Walden that Dutch arrangements for payment in guilders eliminated the immediate issue of releasing Japanese blocked dollar balances, although they also preserved Japan’s dollar holdings. The Netherlands Indies Government was expected to align its export licensing with American policy, but the Department would not guarantee that misunderstandings could not occur. Standard-Vacuum was given a list of products completely embargoed by the United States, allowed to resume license applications for its normal-quota business and encouraged to coordinate its position with Shell.

subfiles.title: Representative Mahon letter concerning proposed Mexican-Japanese barter
subfiles.about: Requests an authoritative ruling on a constituent’s plan to exchange Mexican oil for Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Mahon forwards Andrew Bradford's proposal that Mexico barter oil for Japanese silk and asks if he may participate with State approval.

subfiles.title: Andrew A. Bradford letter proposing oil-for-silk barter
subfiles.about: Proposes supervised Mexican barter with Japan to relieve shortages of silk and rayon.
subfiles.summary: Bradford relays warning that silk shortages could idle textile workers, proposing Mexico trade oil for silk and rayon, perhaps half to the US, or trade directly under American supervision with his help.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to George Mahon on Mexican trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Declines to encourage Bradford’s proposed Mexican barter trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Mexico needs no US permission for trade except frozen funds; the US is not seeking silk via Mexico; Mexico lacks West Coast loading; the Department cannot encourage it but is helping Mexico obtain rayon.

subfiles.title: Mexican Union Refuses Japanese Offer of Silk
subfiles.about: Reports that a Mexican textile union rejected a Japanese silk-for-war-supplies proposal.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Japanese importers offered Mexico silk and rayon for war supplies; the Textile Workers' Union refused, preferring US supplies to protect 7,000 jobs.

subfiles.title: Memorandum citing J. H. Carmical’s estimates of Japanese oil stocks
subfiles.about: Extracts published estimates of Japan’s oil imports, reserves and endurance.
subfiles.summary: Memo citing Carmical: Japan imported 13.5 million barrels of crude from the US and 4.25 million elsewhere last year; stocks about 80 million barrels, two and a half years' supply.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Peruvian molybdenum
subfiles.about: Reports that Peruvian molybdenum deliveries to Japan will stop if Britain purchases the output.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy: Lima says Peruvian molybdenum deliveries to Japan cease if the UK buys it; Britain already agreed; Marris considers the matter settled.

subfiles.title: Finletter letter forwarding the molybdenum settlement
subfiles.about: Forwards the British report that the Peruvian molybdenum problem had been resolved.
subfiles.summary: Finletter sends Bridgman Marris's September 4 letter, which appears to dispose of the Peruvian molybdenum problem.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on a proposed Mexican mercury shipment to Shanghai
subfiles.about: Requests investigation of an apparent attempt to circumvent controls on Mexican mercury exports.
subfiles.summary: British information: attempt to import 11,400 pounds of Mexican mercury to Shanghai, probably for Japan, via Benítez, Malcolm and AGMOL with a $30,000 credit; Reid-Adam asks if it would evade the US-Mexican mercury agreement.

subfiles.title: Braden telegram on Colombian silk and platinum
subfiles.about: Urges rapid action to supply Colombian textile mills and conclude the purchase of Colombian platinum.
subfiles.summary: Braden: Colombia says silk mills need 44,418 pounds quarterly with 31,532 in stock; asks evidence otherwise or rayon assurances; urges buying 62,376 grams of platinum and sending a Metals Reserve representative.

subfiles.title: Statistics on U.S. petroleum exports to Japan, 1937–1941
subfiles.about: Calculates American exports of primary petroleum products to Japan from 1937 through early 1941.
subfiles.summary: Memo totals major petroleum exports to Japan 1937-1940 at 109.178 million barrels, with a Commerce breakdown; first-quarter 1941 exports about 4.735 million barrels.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires telegram on strategic-mineral exports
subfiles.about: Reports Argentine exports of strategic minerals and large mercury and ore shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Buenos Aires: August exports to Japan of tungsten, mica, vanadinite, lithium and gilsonite; the Yamaura Maru carried 5,000 flasks (200 tons) of mercury; origin under inquiry.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese funds for American cotton
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram on a Japanese plan to use frozen U.S. funds to buy American cotton.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japanese officials at Peiping reportedly moved $600,000-$1 million to Volkart Brothers, New York, to buy American cotton for army equipment.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on attempts to obtain industrial diamonds for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports on unsuccessful efforts to procure Mexican bortz for shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bernard Bandler and Sons had Robert Sherman seek commercial diamonds in Mexico after Brazilian bortz difficulties; he failed; the firm sells domestically only for known use and reports to the British Board of Trade.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on possible Japanese lard shipments to Germany
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum suggesting that American lard purchased by Japan might be forwarded to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: April 2, 1941 European Affairs memorandum on lard bought by Japan possibly forwarded to Germany.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Navy inquiry into oil policy toward Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a Navy Department letter requesting information on American oil policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Navy letter of August 9, 1941 on policy governing oil supplied to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Colombian platinum and silk requirements
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram requesting an estimate of Colombia’s silk needs during a three-month adjustment period.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: telegram linking Colombian platinum and silk negotiations, asking how much silk Colombia needs for a three-month adjustment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on cancellation of a Peruvian molybdenum contract with Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch reporting that a molybdenum contract with Japan could be cancelled immediately.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Peruvian despatch 1647 of August 29, 1941 saying the Japan molybdenum contract might be cancelled at once.

subfiles.title: Continuing Efforts of Japanese to Obtain Bolivian Minerals
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, U.S. Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese barter, banking and intermediary schemes intended to secure Bolivian strategic minerals.
subfiles.summary: After threatening to halt textile exports, Japanese representatives proposed buying Bolivian mineral surpluses with local currency or bartering textiles and pottery for minerals, but Bolivian officials showed little interest. The Yokohama Specie Bank then sought dollar facilities through the Banco Central, while a concern owned by Armando H. Ono proposed that Jorge Saenz e Hijos exchange Japanese goods for antimony, lead, copper and quinine. Jenkins believed these schemes had largely been blocked, although Japanese retail stocks and goods at Arica temporarily softened the effect of Japan’s suspension of exports. The despatch also details indirect payment channels through banks and trading concerns in Peru, Chile, Brazil, San Francisco and New York.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum to Yost
subfiles.from: Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary
subfiles.about: Refers an attached matter to Yost as falling within his jurisdiction.
subfiles.summary: Routing memo assuming the matter is within Yost's jurisdiction; no action taken.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Mitsubishi well-drilling machinery
subfiles.about: Reports suspected Mitsubishi efforts to buy well-drilling machinery in Buenos Aires for eventual re-export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy links Mitsubishi efforts in Mexico to a Buenos Aires inquiry for four National Supply drilling machines, specifications sent to Tokyo, suggesting re-export to Japan; prices and specifications supplied.
